transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, honestly, it’s a bit of a mess right now. I’m actually on administrative leave from my job—I work in human resources, mostly handling onboarding and employee experience—and, well, I’m here because of this whole situation with the new onboarding platform launch. See, we had been talking about overhauling the system for months, maybe even a year, and it was just moving so slowly. Too much red tape, too many committees. And a few weeks ago, I just... I saw the path forward so clearly. It felt absolutely necessary, like if we didn't move right that second, we'd lose momentum and lose the best vendors. So, I just pushed ahead. I mean, I really pushed ahead. I committed company funds, signed off on vendor time, scheduled the training modules, all of it. At the time, I felt so bold, so decisive, like I was finally the one getting things done while everyone else was just dragging their feet. But, um, I didn't actually have the final approvals in place. The budget wasn't cleared for that quarter. And now... well, now it’s a disaster. The vendors are confused, my director is furious, and everyone is looking at me, asking what on earth I was thinking. And looking back, I don't even know how to explain it to them, because in that moment, it didn't feel reckless at all, it felt brilliant. But now I'm sitting here, suspended, wondering how I let it get this far.
Can you describe how you were feeling emotionally in the days or hours leading up to the moment you made those decisions? Was it different from how you usually feel?

Well, that’s the thing, it was... it was incredibly different from my baseline. I mean, usually, I’m a very methodical person. You have to be in HR, right? You check the boxes, you follow the compliance guidelines. But for the past few weeks leading up to the launch, it was like a switch flipped. I felt brilliantly alive. I mean, truly, electric. I woke up every day thinking, "This is it. This is the moment I finally show leadership what HR can actually be, not just a support function, but a strategic powerhouse." I had this absolute clarity, this buzzing energy, and I just felt so capable, like I was operating on a completely different frequency than everyone else in the office. 

But then, on the flip side of that—and this is where it got really tricky—if anyone so much as tapped the brakes, I would just snap. I mean, suddenly furious. And I’m not an angry guy, usually! But if a junior associate asked a routine question about the budget, or if someone suggested a tiny, insignificant edit to one of the training module outlines, I would just feel this hot, blinding irritation. It was like they were intentionally trying to sabotage this grand vision I had. I remember one specific Tuesday, my assistant just asked if we should wait for the Q3 numbers before finalizing the vendor contract, and I practically bit her head off. I gave her this whole lecture about how waiting is the enemy of progress, how small-minded thinking was killing the company... I went on for maybe ten minutes. Over a completely standard question! It was just this intense pendulum swing between feeling like a visionary and feeling completely enraged by anyone who wasn't keeping up with my pace.
Can you tell me if this heightened energy and intense focus on pushing the onboarding project forward lasted for a full week or more, or if it came and went in shorter bursts?

A week? Oh, no, no, it was much longer than a week. It didn't come and go in bursts at all, it was... well, honestly, it’s been building for about a solid month. It was this constant, escalating thing. 

It all started—and this is really the context you need to understand the whole situation—it started when they brought in this new executive. He comes over from operations, doesn't even have a formal HR background, which is frustrating enough on its own, but he comes in and almost immediately starts challenging my onboarding redesign. And this is a redesign I had spent the better part of a year researching, benchmarking against top-tier firms, ensuring all the compliance metrics were perfectly aligned. He just waltzes into a strategy meeting and starts picking it apart, challenging the entire framework and the budget allocations. 

And from that exact day, it was like someone lit a fuse in me. It wasn't just a burst of energy here and there. It was every single day for the last month. The momentum just kept compounding, day after day, week after week. I'd be at my desk, or driving, or making dinner, and my mind was just absolutely locked onto pushing this project through, outmaneuvering him, and showing everyone that my vision was exactly what the company needed to survive. So, yeah, it didn't fade in and out. It was a full, intense month of this drive just building and building until I finally just... pulled the trigger on all the contracts.

Can you tell me if, during this time, you had a period where your mood was consistently elevated, expansive, or unusually irritable along with this increased energy or drive, and this was noticeable to others around you?

Well, yes, I’d say it was definitely noticeable. I mean, how could it not be, right? When you’re suddenly operating at that kind of pace, people are going to see it. It wasn't just that I felt energized on the inside; it was completely visible in everything I was doing. I was getting to the office so early, way before anyone else, just buzzing. I’d be walking the floors, back and forth, because sitting at my desk felt... well, it felt almost impossible, honestly. Like I had an actual motor running inside me that wouldn't let me just sit still and look at a screen. 

And it wasn't just pacing, I was actively doing things the whole time. I was constantly rewriting slide decks for the onboarding launch, tweaking the messaging, making it punchier, more aggressive. I was emailing people at all hours—vendors, department heads, even junior staff—just firing off ideas and demands. I was rearranging project timelines, moving milestones up by weeks, sometimes months, because I just couldn't stand the thought of waiting. I was just in constant motion, constantly doing, constantly pushing. So, yes, the mood, the irritation, the absolute drive—it was all there, all at once, and there’s no way the people around me didn't see me practically vibrating with it.

Can you confirm that there was a distinct period lasting at least a week where your mood was clearly different from your usual self—like being unusually high, overly confident, or easily irritated—and during that time you were also acting more driven or energetic in your work or other activities?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, I think I just said that, right? It wasn't just a week, it was that whole month. It was a very, very distinct period. I mean, anyone who knows me—my wife, my team, the people I've worked with for years—they know I'm a very measured guy. You don't survive in HR for fifteen years by being erratic. You just don't. You have to be the calm center of the storm when there's an employee relations issue or a compliance audit. 

But during that month... it was like I was a completely different person. The confidence was just off the charts. I remember looking in the mirror one morning, tying my tie, and actually saying out loud to myself, "You are the only person who sees the big picture here." I really believed it. I felt like I had this crystal-clear vision of the future of the company, and everyone else was just sort of stumbling around in the dark. And the irritation, oh man, the irritation was so intense. If someone couldn't see my vision immediately, if they asked a question that I felt was slowing me down, I just had zero patience. Zero. 

And the energy, the drive... it was non-stop. Like I mentioned, the pacing, the emails at 3 AM... I was completely consumed by it. I wasn't just doing my job, I felt like I was on a crusade to save the company from its own mediocrity. I was completely locked in, operating at 150% capacity, day in and day out, for weeks. So, yes, it was very distinct, very different from my usual self, and it lasted way, way longer than just a week. It was a solid month of just... being on fire.
